newsitem.title: UK: British funds fined for breaking IMRO rules.
newsitem.headline: British funds fined for breaking IMRO rules.

text.p: British investments watchdog the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) on Thursday fined two British fund management firms.
Lincoln Unit Trust Managers Ltd and LIV Ltd were fined a total of 20,000 pounds ($32,400) and have to pay an additional 30,000 pounds in costs for breaching IMRO rules.
The fine is at the lower end of the spectrum for IMRO which has imposed penalties ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands of pounds for rule breakers.
IMRO, one of three "frontline" regulators reporting to Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB), which polices investment firms in Britain.
Its armoury includes being able to fine firms it regulates as much as it deems fit, banning them by revoking their licences, or possibly limiting the scope of their activities.
The watchdog is expected to mete out its largest ever fine in the near future to two fund management units of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG.

It has been investigating what went wrong last year at three of DMG's Morgan Grenfell Asset Management funds. The funds were suspended for several days last September when irregularities were discovered in valuations.

Deutsche Bank has injected 180 million pounds into the funds and has since agreed a 200 million pound compensation package with IMRO for those of the 90,000 retail investors who were disadvantaged by the affair. Compensation is due to be paid by the end of the month.
The largest fine so far imposed by IMRO was a 750,000 pound penalty against Invesco in June 1993. But the DMG fine is widely expected to be in the region of a million pounds.

Having brought the question of compensation to a hasty conclusion, IMRO will concentrate on internal corporate failings at Morgan Grenfell International Funds Management and Morgan Grenfell Unit Trust Managers -- the two firms it regulates -- rather than individuals when it concludes the first stage of its report.

IMRO said Gloucester-based Lincoln, formerly Lincoln Fund Managers Ltd, and LIV, formerly Lincoln Investment Management Ltd, did not bank PEP (personal equity plan) customers' money on time and did not have adequate compliance monitoring in some areas.

Lincoln breached IMRO rules by not paying the money it received from around 700 PEP applications, around 25 percent of the total, into a client money bank account within the required period between January 1 1994 and January 31 1995.

Between April 1993 and February 1995 Lincoln "did not have adequate procedures for monitoring that client money was banked properly nor that orders were executed as soon as reasonably practicable", IMRO said.

And LIV "did not have adequate procedures for monitoring that investments were suitable nor that allocations were made in accordance with uniform standards and procedures, nor that best execution was provided," the watchdog added.

IMRO said that at the time of the breaches LIV was a fund management company with approximately 1.1 billion pounds under management while Lincoln, an authorised trust manager, managed nine trust units and PEPs and had around 479 million pounds under management.
It said both firms had agreed to the settlement of disciplinary proceedings and had remedied the deficiencies.

Regulatory sources say there has been an increase in staff turnover at Britain's frontline regulators in recent months due to the attractive packages on offer and uncertainty over possible changes to the system of financial regulation if the opposition Labour party wins the election on May 1.
